Migrate SQL Server (VM) to Azure SQL Database with DACPAC and BCP

Nithin Sunke · November 1, 2026 · 20 min read

Lab 3 of the Azure SQL Database migration series: deploy the schema with a DACPAC, then bulk-copy 16.8 million rows table by table with BCP. Every error along the way is documented: platform checks, certificates, a serverless database that was asleep, and the foreign-key and row-count checks that caught the damage.

How this method works

Instead of one package with schema and data together (BACPAC, Lab 1) or a managed service (DMS, Lab 2), this method moves the schema and the data separately:

SQL Server (VM) ──SqlPackage Extract──▶ scsbank.dacpac ──SqlPackage Publish──▶ Azure SQL DB (empty tables)
SQL Server (VM) ──bcp out (per table)──▶ *.dat files   ──bcp in (per table)──▶ Azure SQL DB (data)
  • DACPAC: a schema-only package, like Oracle expdp CONTENT=METADATA_ONLY.
  • BCP (Bulk Copy Program): exports each table to a file and bulk-loads it, like expdp CONTENT=DATA_ONLY or SQL*Loader.

Why choose it: you control each table, so you can rerun one failed table, load big tables in parallel, review the schema script before deploying, and build incremental loads on top. The trade-off is that you own all the checking. As this lab shows, BCP failures can be silent.

Lab environment

ComponentDetails
SourceSQL Server 2025 (17.0) on Windows VM MSSQLSRV01, database scsbank
Targetcisql01.database.windows.net, empty free-offer database scsbank (General Purpose Serverless, 2 vCores)
ToolsSqlPackage 170.4, BCP and sqlcmd 17.0.1000.7 (ODBC Driver 18), VS Code with mssql
Data17 tables, 10 schemas, 16,760,354 rows, about 2 GB of native-format files

Prepare the VM

BCP is installed with SQL Server. Check its version:

bcp -v

Create a working folder with data and logs subfolders:

mkdir B:\BCP_EXPORT\data, B:\BCP_EXPORT\logs

The target is a new, empty SQL database (Free offer) named scsbank on cisql01. The VM's public IP is already in the server firewall (from Lab 1).

Move the schema (DACPAC)

1Extract schema only

sqlpackage /Action:Extract `
  /SourceServerName:localhost /SourceDatabaseName:scsbank `
  /SourceTrustServerCertificate:True `
  /TargetFile:"B:\BCP_EXPORT\scsbank.dacpac" `
  /p:ExtractAllTableData=False

2Preview the deployment script

The first attempt failed:

Error: A project which specifies SQL Server 2025 or Azure SQL Database Managed Instance as the target platform cannot be published to Microsoft Azure SQL Database v12.
Why: a DACPAC records the platform it was extracted from. SqlPackage refuses to deploy it to a different platform by default.
Fix: add /p:AllowIncompatiblePlatform=True. This only skips the platform check. Features Azure SQL Database truly doesn't support will still fail and be named.
sqlpackage /Action:Script `
  /SourceFile:"B:\BCP_EXPORT\scsbank.dacpac" `
  /TargetServerName:cisql01.database.windows.net /TargetDatabaseName:scsbank `
  /TargetUser:nsunke /TargetPassword:'<password>' `
  /p:AllowIncompatiblePlatform=True `
  /OutputPath:"B:\BCP_EXPORT\scsbank_deploy.sql"

Open scsbank_deploy.sql and check it before publishing. It should contain only CREATE statements, with no DROPs.

3Publish the schema

sqlpackage /Action:Publish `
  /SourceFile:"B:\BCP_EXPORT\scsbank.dacpac" `
  /TargetServerName:cisql01.database.windows.net /TargetDatabaseName:scsbank `
  /TargetUser:nsunke /TargetPassword:'<password>' `
  /p:AllowIncompatiblePlatform=True /p:BlockOnPossibleDataLoss=True
The DACPAC also included the database user dmsuser from Lab 2 ("Creating User [dmsuser]"). A DACPAC carries database users and role memberships. Review them, and drop any you don't want on the target.

4Verify: 17 empty tables

SELECT s.name, t.name, SUM(p.rows) AS row_count
FROM sys.tables t JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id=s.schema_id
JOIN sys.partitions p ON t.object_id=p.object_id AND p.index_id IN (0,1)
GROUP BY s.name, t.name ORDER BY 1,2;

Stop writes on the source

BCP only reads from the source, so read-only mode is safe here. Check the editor header shows the source connection (onprmisesql | 81.208.167.201), not cisql01. That mix-up broke Lab 2.

ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET READ_ONLY WITH ROLLBACK IMMEDIATE;

Export data (bcp out)

bcp_out.ps1 lists the tables with sqlcmd and exports each one in native format:

$src  = "localhost"
$db   = "scsbank"
$dir  = "B:\BCP_EXPORT\data"
$logs = "B:\BCP_EXPORT\logs"

$tables = sqlcmd -S $src -d $db -E -C -h -1 -W -Q "SET NOCOUNT ON; SELECT s.name + '.' + t.name FROM sys.tables t JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id=s.schema_id ORDER BY 1"

foreach ($t in $tables | Where-Object { $_ -and $_.Trim() -ne "" }) {
    $t = $t.Trim()
    Write-Host "Exporting $t ..."
    bcp "$db.$t" out "$dir\$t.dat" -S $src -T -N -u -o "$logs\out_$t.log"
}
Get-ChildItem $dir | Select-Object Name, @{n='MB';e={[math]::Round($_.Length/1MB,1)}}

The first run failed straight away:

Error: SSL Provider: The certificate chain was issued by an authority that is not trusted.
Why: ODBC Driver 18 encrypts connections and validates the certificate by default. The local SQL Server uses a self-signed certificate.
Fix: trust the server certificate for the local connection: -C for sqlcmd, -u for bcp 18. Don't use these against Azure, whose certificate is trusted.
FlagMeaning
-TWindows authentication on the source
-NNative format: fastest, and exact data types between SQL Server engines
-uTrust the server certificate (bcp 18, local source only)
-oWrite output to a log file. Note this also hides errors from the console.

Import data (bcp in)

$tgt  = "tcp:cisql01.database.windows.net,1433"
$db   = "scsbank"
$user = "nsunke"
$pwd  = Read-Host "Azure SQL password"
$dir  = "B:\BCP_EXPORT\data"

Get-ChildItem $dir -Filter *.dat | ForEach-Object {
    $t = $_.BaseName
    Write-Host "Loading $t ..."
    bcp "$t" in "$($_.FullName)" -S $tgt -d $db -U $user -P $pwd `
        -N -E -b 50000 -h "TABLOCK" -o "B:\BCP_EXPORT\logs\in_$t.log"
}
FlagWhy
-d scsbankAzure SQL Database doesn't accept db.schema.table names, so pass the database separately
-EKeep identity values. Without it, IDs are regenerated and the foreign-key links break.
-b 50000Commit every 50,000 rows to keep transactions small on a 2-vCore database
-h "TABLOCK"Faster bulk load
Read-Host echoes what you type. The password appeared in plain text on screen, and in my screenshots (blurred here). Use Read-Host -AsSecureString, as in the improved script below.

I then checked the logs:

Select-String -Path B:\BCP_EXPORT\logs\*.log -Pattern "rows copied","Error" | Select-Object Filename, Line

Easy to miss at a glance. The validation steps below caught it.

Re-validate constraints, and what they caught

BCP skips foreign-key and CHECK constraint checks during the load, which leaves those constraints untrusted. You re-check them afterwards. That re-check is also your first data-integrity test.

Error: sp_MSforeachtable doesn't exist in Azure

Fix: generate the statements with dynamic SQL instead:

DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) = N'';
SELECT @sql += N'ALTER TABLE ' + QUOTENAME(s.name) + N'.' + QUOTENAME(t.name)
             + N' WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT ALL;' + CHAR(10)
FROM sys.tables t JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
WHERE t.is_ms_shipped = 0;
PRINT @sql;
EXEC sp_executesql @sql;

Error: FK_Card_Account conflict

Diagnosis: compare parent and child, and count the orphans:

SELECT 'Account' t, COUNT(*), MIN(AccountID), MAX(AccountID) FROM Account.Account
UNION ALL
SELECT 'Card', COUNT(*), MIN(AccountID), MAX(AccountID) FROM Card.Card;

SELECT COUNT(*) AS orphan_cards
FROM Card.Card c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Account.Account a WHERE a.AccountID = c.AccountID);

Fix: reload Account.Account:

Check every foreign key at once

Rather than fixing one error at a time, this query lists every broken relationship and its parent table:

DECLARE @sql NVARCHAR(MAX) = N'';
SELECT @sql += CASE WHEN @sql = N'' THEN N'' ELSE N' UNION ALL ' END +
  N'SELECT ''' + fk.name + N''' AS fk, ''' + cs.name + N'.' + ct.name + N''' AS child, ''' +
  ps.name + N'.' + pt.name + N''' AS parent, COUNT(*) AS orphans FROM ' +
  QUOTENAME(cs.name) + N'.' + QUOTENAME(ct.name) + N' c WHERE c.' + QUOTENAME(cc.name) +
  N' IS NOT NULL AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ' + QUOTENAME(ps.name) + N'.' + QUOTENAME(pt.name) +
  N' p WHERE p.' + QUOTENAME(pc.name) + N' = c.' + QUOTENAME(cc.name) + N')' + CHAR(10)
FROM sys.foreign_keys fk
JOIN sys.foreign_key_columns fkc ON fkc.constraint_object_id = fk.object_id
JOIN sys.tables ct  ON ct.object_id = fk.parent_object_id
JOIN sys.schemas cs ON cs.schema_id = ct.schema_id
JOIN sys.columns cc ON cc.object_id = ct.object_id AND cc.column_id = fkc.parent_column_id
JOIN sys.tables pt  ON pt.object_id = fk.referenced_object_id
JOIN sys.schemas ps ON ps.schema_id = pt.schema_id
JOIN sys.columns pc ON pc.object_id = pt.object_id AND pc.column_id = fkc.referenced_column_id;
SET @sql = N'SELECT * FROM (' + @sql + N') x WHERE orphans > 0 ORDER BY parent;';
EXEC sp_executesql @sql;

With both parents reloaded, every constraint validates and none are untrusted:

The table the foreign keys couldn't catch

The constraint checks passed, but the row-count check showed one more empty table:

No table references Audit.LoginEvent, so an empty LoginEvent breaks no foreign key. The FK check only catches empty parent tables. Only row counts catch everything.

Root cause: serverless auto-pause

The LoginEvent log finally showed what went wrong:

Error: TCP Provider: Timeout error [258] … Unable to complete login process due to delay in login response … Login timeout expired.
Why: the free-tier database is serverless and auto-pauses after 15 idle minutes. Resuming takes 30–60 seconds, and BCP's default login timeout is 15 s. The script loads tables alphabetically, so the first three, Account.Account, Account.Beneficiary and Audit.LoginEvent, timed out while the database was waking. By the fourth it was online, and all the rest succeeded.
Fix: wake the database first, and give BCP a longer login timeout (-l 120).
bcp "Audit.LoginEvent" in "B:\BCP_EXPORT\data\Audit.LoginEvent.dat" `
  -S tcp:cisql01.database.windows.net,1433 -d scsbank -U nsunke -P $pwd `
  -N -E -b 50000 -h "TABLOCK" -l 120 -o "B:\BCP_EXPORT\logs\in_Audit.LoginEvent_retry.log"

Improved bcp_in.ps1

This version hides the password, wakes the database, uses a longer login timeout, retries failed tables, and prints a summary:

$tgt = "tcp:cisql01.database.windows.net,1433"; $db = "scsbank"; $user = "nsunke"
$sec = Read-Host "Azure SQL password" -AsSecureString
$pwd = [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::PtrToStringAuto(
         [Runtime.InteropServices.Marshal]::SecureStringToBSTR($sec))

# 1. Wake the serverless database
sqlcmd -S $tgt -d $db -U $user -P $pwd -l 120 -Q "SELECT 1" | Out-Null

# 2. Load each table, retry up to 3 times
Get-ChildItem B:\BCP_EXPORT\data -Filter *.dat | ForEach-Object {
    $t = $_.BaseName; $log = "B:\BCP_EXPORT\logs\in_$t.log"
    for ($i = 1; $i -le 3; $i++) {
        bcp "$t" in "$($_.FullName)" -S $tgt -d $db -U $user -P $pwd `
            -N -E -b 50000 -h "TABLOCK" -l 120 -o $log
        if (Select-String -Path $log -Pattern "rows copied" -Quiet) { Write-Host "OK    $t"; break }
        Write-Host "RETRY $t ($i)"; Start-Sleep 30
    }
}

# 3. Summary: every table must appear here
Select-String -Path B:\BCP_EXPORT\logs\in_*.log -Pattern "rows copied|Error" | Select Filename, Line

Retrying is safe for failures that happen before any rows go in, such as login timeouts. If a load fails partway through, delete that table's rows before retrying, or you'll get duplicate-key errors.

Final validation

SELECT s.name, t.name, SUM(p.rows) AS row_count
FROM sys.tables t JOIN sys.schemas s ON t.schema_id = s.schema_id
JOIN sys.partitions p ON t.object_id = p.object_id AND p.index_id IN (0,1)
GROUP BY s.name, t.name ORDER BY 1,2;

SELECT type_desc, COUNT(*) FROM sys.objects
WHERE is_ms_shipped = 0 GROUP BY type_desc ORDER BY 1;

Then re-run the constraint script once more, now that LoginEvent is loaded, and confirm SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sys.foreign_keys WHERE is_not_trusted = 1 returns 0. Finally, reopen the source:

ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET READ_WRITE;   -- on MSSQLSRV01

Delete the .dat files when you're done. They hold the full dataset unencrypted.

All errors and fixes

#ErrorCauseFix
1Unrecognized command line argument 'SourceServiceName'Typo/SourceServerName
2Project targeting SQL Server 2025 cannot be published to Azure SQL Database v12DACPAC records the source platform/p:AllowIncompatiblePlatform=True
3SSL Provider: certificate chain not trustedODBC 18 validates certificates; the local server is self-signed-C (sqlcmd) and -u (bcp), source only
4Login failed for user 'sa' (18456)Wrong password, State 8 in the error logUse Windows authentication or a named admin login; keep sa disabled
5Could not find stored procedure 'sp_MSforeachtable'Undocumented procedure, not in Azure SQL DatabaseDynamic SQL over sys.tables
6Msg 547: FK_Card_Account conflictAccount.Account empty (load timed out)Reload the parent with -E
7Msg 547: FK_Txn_Beneficiary conflictAccount.Beneficiary empty (load timed out)Reload the parent
8Audit.LoginEvent 0 rows, no error anywhereLoad timed out; the table isn't a FK parentRow-count validation, then reload with -l 120
9Login timeout expired / TCP timeout 258Serverless database auto-pausedWake it first; -l 120; retry loop

Troubleshooting checklist for BCP migrations

  1. Never trust the console. With -o, BCP prints nothing. Check that every in_*.log ends with N rows copied, and count them: 17 tables need 17 lines.
  2. Compare row counts for every table on source and target. This is the only check that catches everything.
  3. Re-validate constraints with WITH CHECK CHECK CONSTRAINT ALL. A conflict means an empty or partial parent, missing -E, or bad data in the source.
  4. Read the errors behind the error. The SQL error log gives the real login failure state (8 = wrong password, 7 = disabled, 58 = Windows-only mode). The BCP log gives the real load failure.
  5. Serverless targets: warm up before loading, and use generous login timeouts.
  6. Re-loading: an empty table can be loaded directly. For a partial table, DELETE it first. You can't TRUNCATE a table that foreign keys reference.

Security lesson: an exposed SQL port

While investigating the sa login failure, the SQL Server error log showed something more serious than a wrong password:

These weren't my attempts. They came from an unfamiliar IP, every couple of seconds, before I'd tried to log in at all. That's an automated brute-force attack: the VM's port 1433 was open to the internet, and bots scan for exposed SQL Servers constantly.

  • Disable sa (ALTER LOGIN sa DISABLE) and use named admin logins.
  • Close 1433 to the internet in the cloud security list or NSG, or restrict it to your own IP. BCP, SqlPackage and the integration runtime run on the VM and connect out, so none of them need inbound 1433.
  • Check for successful logins from unknown IPs: EXEC xp_readerrorlog 0, 1, N'Login succeeded'.
  • Keep passwords out of screenshots and rotate any that leak.

Making it incremental

To shrink downtime, bulk-load while the application is still running, then copy only the changes at cutover. How you find the changes depends on the table:

Table typeExampleHow to find the delta
Static referenceProduct.BankProduct, Org.BranchReload fully at cutover
Insert-onlyAudit.LoginEvent, Txn.AccountTransactionIdentity or date watermark (WHERE ID > @max_at_load)
UpdatedCustomer.Customer, Account.Accountrowversion column or a reliable ModifiedDate
Updated and deletedCard.Card, Account.BeneficiaryChange Tracking (CHANGETABLE gives I/U/D per key)
Unknown or third-partyAnyHash compare, or use replication or DMS instead
-- Change Tracking: enable before the initial load
ALTER DATABASE scsbank SET CHANGE_TRACKING = ON (CHANGE_RETENTION = 3 DAYS, AUTO_CLEANUP = ON);
ALTER TABLE Card.Card ENABLE CHANGE_TRACKING;
SELECT CHANGE_TRACKING_CURRENT_VERSION();       -- note it, e.g. 1500

-- At cutover: every insert/update/delete since then
SELECT ct.SYS_CHANGE_OPERATION, ct.CardID, c.*
FROM CHANGETABLE(CHANGES Card.Card, 1500) ct
LEFT JOIN Card.Card c ON c.CardID = ct.CardID;

Load the delta into a staging table, then apply it on the target with MERGE for inserts and updates, plus DELETE for deletes. Apply parents before children, and process deletes children first. If many tables need update and delete tracking, use Azure Data Factory with Change Tracking, or transactional replication, rather than hand-built scripts.

Results and takeaways

BACPAC (Lab 1)DMS (Lab 2)DACPAC + BCP (Lab 3)
SchemaIncludedOptional, automaticSeparate, reviewable script
Data unitWhole databaseSelected tablesPer table, files you control
Rerun one tableNoNoYes
Parallel loadNoYes, automaticYes, manual
Error visibilityFails loudlyPortal per tableSilent unless you check
Incremental possibleNoNo (Azure SQL DB)Yes, with deltas
LeftoversNoneTracking table, SHIRData files to delete
  • Schema and data travel separately, which gives the most control: review the deploy script, rerun single tables, and parallelise big ones.
  • That control comes with responsibility. BCP will happily report nothing while three tables stay empty. Logs, constraint re-checks and row counts together are what made this migration trustworthy.
  • Serverless targets sleep. Warm them up and set generous login timeouts for any scripted load.
  • Always use -E with identity columns, and re-trust constraints after the load.
  • A migration VM is still a server on the internet. Lock down ports and logins before you start.
